Dear Uday,
Summer update from your favourite cousin! We made a list and did ALL of it: the new food lane near the station (the paneer rolls!), three films in one week, the late-night kulfi walk, and Mitali's birthday at the lake. I made two new friends from the kulfi walk alone. Mummy says her daughter lights up the house when I'm in a good mood, which is always, so.
Okay, confession. Our science project was due on Monday. I knew for a month. Every time I sat down it felt so boring compared to everything else. I finished it on Sunday night, badly. Ma'am wrote, "You are capable of more, Pallavi." That stung a bit, I won't lie.
I don't want to stop having fun. It's the best part of me. But maybe fun can't be the only thing on the list.
Write back and tell me about hostel food. Is it as bad as you said?
Pallavi

qa.a: It stung; she felt a bit ashamed because she knew she had left the project till Sunday night even though she had a month.

qa.a: Uday would likely see Pallavi as warm and full of life, the fun one, while noticing she is starting to think about balance.

"Okay, so for the school magazine, you want to know why I'm 'the fun one'? I'm Yamini, Class 12, and honestly I've always been like this.
I plan everything. The class picnic to the waterfall? Me. Movie Fridays at my house? Me. When Ramesh's grandfather passed away, I organised a samosa evening for his family and just sat with him. Fun isn't only laughing. It's being together.

That hurt. So now I plan the fun and I plan the boring stuff too. Tuesday and Thursday evenings are for chemistry, no exceptions. Ramesh says I'm still the fun girl, just the fun girl who passes."

Friday. Rajni, fifteen, had a science test on Monday. She told herself: Sunday. Then Zubin texted about the new film. She went, laughed so hard her popcorn spilled, and walked home singing.
Saturday. The whole group went to the food street. Pani puri, kulfi, a long walk by the lake. Rajni felt light and happy. At night she opened her science book, looked at one page, and closed it.
Monday. The test paper swam in front of her eyes. She left three questions blank.
Walking out, Zubin said, "Worth it though, right? The film?"
Rajni laughed, but it came out thin. The film had been wonderful. The test had not.

Hafsa, your Ammi says you've been at the mall every evening. Let me tell you about the boy I was at fifteen.
In old Hyderabad, I lived for fun. Cricket in the lane till dark. Irani chai and Osmania biscuits at the café with my gang. Every new film on the first day, even if I had to sell my comics for the ticket.
My friends loved me. I was the one who made plans. I still think that was a gift.
But I failed Class 10 maths the first time. I had not opened the book for months. My father didn't shout. He just looked tired.
That summer, I kept the cricket, but I made a rule: two hours of maths first, then the lane. I passed in the supplementary exam.
I'm Santosh, beta. Keep the fun. Just don't let it hold the steering wheel.

qa.q: Which subject did Santosh fail in Class 10?
qa.a: Maths.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when his father just looked tired?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and sorry, realising his fun had cost him and disappointed his father.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped young Santosh, and why?
qa.a: Making a rule of two hours of maths before cricket helped, because he kept the fun but stopped it from crowding out work.

qa.q: How might Santosh's father have felt that year?
qa.a: He probably felt worried and disappointed, too tired to shout about the failed exam.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a teenager, his love of fun brought friends but crowded out study.
